# Nuclear weapons (`nuclear_weapons`)

<!-- generated by scripts/build_techtree.py from techtree/core/military.yaml — do not edit -->

- Category: Warfare, security & deterrence (`military`)
- Deps: needs nuclear_fission; helped by nuclear_reactor, military_aviation, rocket_spaceflight
- Core idea: Nuclear fission releases energy from atomic nuclei. Scientists recognised the possibility of a rapid chain reaction in 1939–40. Turning that discovery into a weapon required a vast wartime industrial programme. The US-led Manhattan Project drew on British and Canadian cooperation and the work of researchers from many countries. Trinity in July 1945 was the first nuclear test. In August the United States used nuclear weapons against Hiroshima and Nagasaki. Blast, fire and radiation killed civilians on a massive scale. The subsequent arms race and the risk of catastrophic retaliation reshaped international politics.
- Pitfalls:
  - Thinking the secret is a formula; the principle was published in 1945 and the difficulty is industrial
  - Natural uranium does not explode; it is nearly all the wrong isotope
  - Underrating fire, radiation and fallout, which add greatly to the deaths from blast
  - Assuming a monopoly lasts; the first Soviet test in 1949 ended the US monopoly
  - A player who 'brings the bomb' to an early era brings only an idea that nobody can use, plus the knowledge that it changes diplomacy
- History: europe: 1933 – Szilard conceives the neutron chain reaction; 1938–1939 – fission discovered and explained (Hahn, Strassmann, Meitner, Frisch); 1940 – Frisch-Peierls memorandum shows a bomb is feasible; 1949 – first Soviet test; 1952 – first British test; americas: 1942–1945 – Manhattan Project; 16 July 1945 – Trinity test; 1952 – first thermonuclear test; east_asia: 6 and 9 August 1945 – Hiroshima and Nagasaki, the only use in war; china: 1964 – first Chinese test; india: 1974 – first Indian test
- Read:
  - Richard Rhodes, The Making of the Atomic Bomb (1986)
  - Henry DeWolf Smyth, Atomic Energy for Military Purposes (1945)
